item.title: Inside New Zealand’s Telco Data Breaches
item.description:
An Auckland ransomware case and three years of Spark disclosures reveal how little the headline numbers can tell customers about their own exposure.

In December 2024, Compass Communications detected unauthorised access to its systems. The Auckland telecommunications provider brought in outside security specialists and notified New Zealand’s Privacy Commissioner. The ransomware group RA World claimed it had stolen 250 gigabytes of data.

The attackers also posted a 26.9 MB sample. Cyber Daily reported that it contained service agreements, financial statements and customer banking details. Compass confirmed the intrusion and said its initial investigation suggested some customer information may have been accessed. It said it would contact customers directly where it identified an impact. The company’s statement gave no customer count or verified figure for the volume of data taken. 

The banking details in the reported sample gave customers a more concrete reason to pay attention than the 250 GB claim. An archive can contain several documents for a single account, duplicates of the same file and records unrelated to customers. Its size gives little indication of how many people are affected or whether the records belong to current or former customers.

Three Years of Breach Reports at Spark

Spark New Zealand’s annual reports provide a different view. In FY24, staff reported 228 data breaches for investigation. Of those, 30, or about 13%, met the threshold for notifying affected people and the Privacy Commissioner. Spark said most of those cases involved fraudsters using personal information they had obtained elsewhere, including through phishing or compromised online accounts. 

Staff reported 156 breaches for investigation in FY25 and 167 in FY26. The privacy sections of those two annual reports gave no count of how many cases met the notification threshold. Both totals cover the company as a whole, with no separate figures for home broadband customers. Internal reports rose between the two years, but the disclosures leave it unclear whether serious breaches rose as well. 

Spark had previously disclosed a specific example. In FY21, it notified customers and the Privacy Commissioner about unauthorised access to some MySpark and Xtra Mail accounts. Spark said customers had reused their login details on other platforms, where the credentials were harvested after those platforms were compromised. At Compass, the company detected unauthorised access inside its own systems. The two cases raise different questions about what an intruder could see, change or copy. 

The Gap Between a Breach Count and a Customer Notice

New Zealand’s Office of the Privacy Commissioner recorded 1,093 privacy breach notifications in 2024/25, up 27% from the previous year. Of those, 591 were classified as serious, up 43%. Those figures cover all sectors. The regulator also reported that 71% of serious breaches were notified to its office within 72 hours, compared with 60% the previous year. 

Under New Zealand’s Privacy Act, organisations must notify the Commissioner as soon as practicable when a breach has caused or is likely to cause serious harm. The Commissioner expects notification within 72 hours of an organisation becoming aware that a breach is notifiable. Organisations generally must also notify affected people, subject to exceptions. A customer may receive details directly that never appear in a company’s annual report or public statement. 

“An old broadband bill can tell a scammer who your provider is, where you live and what you usually pay. That’s enough to make a fake overdue bill look real. When a provider says ‘customer information’ was exposed, people need to know whether that means an email address or a copy of their bill,” says Tomas Novosad, founder of Fibre Broadband NZ.

In the Compass case, a claimed file size made headlines while the number of affected customers was still unclear. Spark’s annual reports offer company-wide totals, with less detail in the two latest years about how many cases reached the notification threshold. For customers, three details would put those numbers in perspective: the types of data involved, the period the records cover and the number of affected accounts.

(Photo by Denny Müller on Unsplash)

item.title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product Security
item.description:
Columbus, Ohio, United States, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates

Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains.

The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it.

In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability.

Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see.

“Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund. “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”

“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking. “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.”

Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031, Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it.

Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD., a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: “The depth of Finite State’s binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what’s in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable.”

Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.”

Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category.

By continuously generating SBOMs, VEX, and signed compliance packages, Finite State enables connected device companies across industries such as medical devices and automotive to meet evolving regulations, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and deliver continuous compliance at speed.

item.title: OffSec Celebrates 20 Years of Practitioner-Built Training From the Creators of Kali Linux and OSCP
item.description:
New York, USA, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Meet the rest of OffSec as the company brings its hands-on approach to entire cyber teams.

Kali Linux. OSCP. Try Harder. For 20 years, OffSec has set the standard for the tools security practitioners use, the skills they prove, and the mindset they bring to the work. This month OffSec is marking its 20th anniversary as a global leader in hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications for individuals and enterprise security teams. 

“Our founders built an incredible brand and an incredible product,” said OffSec CEO Ning Wang. “Our mission has stayed the same. We develop critical thinkers, cyber warriors, and problem solvers who are ready to excel in their jobs under stress. Hands-on is the only way we believe you can effectively train someone.”

Built by the People Who Do the Work

OffSec began in 2006 when cybercrime was becoming big business. OffSec grew out of the security community, founded by practitioners who believed the best way to teach cybersecurity was to share what they’d learned through hands-on experience. That origin story still shapes how OffSec develops cybersecurity practitioners and teams. Through hands-on training with real systems, learners build practical skills, strengthen their problem-solving abilities, and gain the confidence to tackle challenges when the obvious approach fails.

The Tools Practitioners Use

BackTrack Linux brought penetration testing tools together in one open-source platform. In 2013, OffSec rebuilt it as Kali Linux, a free environment for penetration testing, research, forensics, and reverse engineering. In 2023, Kali Purple extended it to defenders.

The Standard Practitioners Prove Themselves Against

OSCP earned its reputation as the gold standard in penetration testing certifications because candidates must work through live systems, adapt their approach, and document what they accomplish. Employers trust it as evidence of real capability. For many practitioners, it is a career-defining milestone. OSCP+ added a renewable credential in 2024. Now, for a limited time, individual practitioners can save 20% off of Learn One annual subscription.

The Research and Practice They Learn From

In 2009, OffSec launched the Exploit Database, a non-profit, public-service archive of public exploits, proof-of-concept (PoC) code, shellcode, and security papers, which it still maintains as a free resource. It also acquired the open-source training project VulnHub, offers free labs in Proving Grounds Play, and recently added HackTrack. HackTrack offers live weekly training over a 10-week stretch. The first round of HackTrack focused on OSCP and was offered free to those with a Learn One or Course and Certification Bundle. A new HackTrack focused on OSAI is set to launch soon. 

Along the way, Try Harder became the security community’s shorthand for the persistence and dedication that a career in cybersecurity demands. In October 2026 at Singapore International Cyber Week, CEO Wang urged her Women in Cyber keynote audience to do hard things early that build confidence and resilience, noting, “If you don’t struggle through something, you will never become really great at it,” she said. 

The Technology Looks Different. The Challenge Feels Familiar

Attackers now use AI to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at speeds unimaginable 20 years ago. The time between a vendor patch and a working exploit continues to shrink. Cybersecurity skills gaps remain a growing challenge. According to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 95% of organizations report at least one skills gap, with 59% describing those gaps as critical or significant, up from 44% in 2024. These findings reinforce the need to move beyond once-a-year training toward continuous, hands-on skill development, an approach rooted in OffSec’s philosophy since day one.

“Frontier AI models are evolving at unbelievable speed. If you don’t keep up, you won’t be able to do the job,” said CEO Wang. “Certification still assesses capability. But you need to constantly upskill your teams so they are ready to defend your organization. It is simply no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Meet the Rest of Offsec: Training for the Whole Security Team

OffSec has grown from a specialist offensive security provider into a full cybersecurity learning and workforce development portfolio. Every course teaches the why, the what, and the how so practitioners learn to think through problems they have never seen. Through Learn Enterprise, OffSec’s hands-on training platform for enterprise security teams, organizations bring that approach to every member of their security team. The platform includes:

  • 14 certifications from foundational to expert level
  • 125+ customizable learning paths
  • 750+ labs
  • 8,000+ hours of content
  • Framework mapping to NICE, DCWF, SCyWF, ECSF, and more
  • Flexible licenses
  • Workforce leadership reporting

In 2026, OffSec added Live Training, which brings its instructors on site to work with security teams in realistic scenarios. OffSec has provided this training to more than two dozen organizations and hundreds of learners. 

OffSec’s AI Training Priorities

CEO Wang calls AI-era learning OffSec’s top priority. “To fight AI you have to use AI,” said CEO Wang. “Your red team and your blue team both need to be AI literate. Next year, we will release new and updated courses that modernize our training for the AI age.”

Preview OffSec’s Learn Enterprise platform, then request a personalized demo to explore how it can support your team’s training goals at: https://www.offsec.com/business/enterprise-solutions/. 

About OffSec

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

That origin story still shapes how OffSec develops cybersecurity practitioners and teams. Through hands-on training with real systems, learners build practical skills, strengthen their problem-solving abilities, and gain the confidence to tackle challenges when the obvious approach fails.

The Tools Practitioners Use

BackTrack Linux brought penetration testing tools together in one open-source platform. In 2013, OffSec rebuilt it as Kali Linux, a free environment for penetration testing, research, forensics, and reverse engineering. In 2023, Kali Purple extended it to defenders.

The Standard Practitioners Prove Themselves Against

OSCP earned its reputation as the gold standard in penetration testing certifications because candidates must work through live systems, adapt their approach, and document what they accomplish. Employers trust it as evidence of real capability. For many practitioners, it is a career-defining milestone. OSCP+ added a renewable credential in 2024. Now, for a limited time, individual practitioners can save 20% off of Learn One annual subscription.

The Research and Practice They Learn From

item.title: One Identity Unveils Active Roles 8.6 with Enhanced Security and Administration
item.description:
Alisa Viejo, California, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Active Roles 8.6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades 

One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8.6, strengthening secure and streamlined Active Directory administration with cumulative platform improvements, expanded API capabilities and greater authentication flexibility.

Active Roles 8.6, updated July 27, 2026, focuses on security and cumulative platform improvements. It fixes an RSTS configuration security issue and supersedes versions 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Compared with Active Roles 8.2.1 SP6, One Identity says 8.6 incorporates the features, enhancements and resolved issues delivered across that intervening release line. See the Active Roles 8.6 Release Notes.

The recent improvements are therefore best described as an administrator and integration experience upgrade, rather than a new visual redesign. The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication. 

Active Roles 8.6: Familiar Administration Meets Greater Flexibility and Consolidation 

Those upgrades complement one of Active Roles’ most recognizable usability strengths: a flexible, configurable UI that can be tailored to individual users and personas. Its thick-client interface is designed to resemble the familiar Microsoft Active Directory experience, helping reduce the learning curve for experienced AD administrators. 

The broader experience centers on consolidation, with a single console spanning Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 helping administrators avoid constantly switching between separate management environments. Together with PowerShell and VBScript support, the product keeps familiar tools and interaction patterns at the center of the administrator experience. 

This combination of configurable views, familiar administration and centralized control supports Active Roles’ position among top Active Directory management solutions. 

#1 Peerspot Position Strengthens the Ease-of-Administration Story 

PeerSpot currently ranks Active Roles by One Identity #1 in Active Directory Management, with an 8.5/10 rating based on 92 reviews. It also reports the largest category mindshare at 11.7%, up from 10.4% year over year, and identifies Active Roles as the category’s most popular solution by searches.  

The PeerSpot assessment highlights automated user provisioning, lifecycle management, role-based access control, password resets and streamlined account management among capabilities that reduce manual effort. 

Feature in focus: Administrator experience with Active Roles 8.6 

Active Roles 8.6 is an administrator-experience evolution, combining cumulative security, API and authentication improvements with the product’s established configurable UI, familiar Microsoft-style experience and consolidated hybrid administration.

One Identity delivers trusted identity security for enterprises worldwide to protect and simplify access to digital identities. item.description:
Alisa Vijeo, California, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

One Identity today unveiled Safeguard 9.0, a major update designed to reduce the infrastructure, administrative overhead and operational complexity associated with enterprise privileged access management.

As privileged access management becomes more critical and complex, One Identity Safeguard continues to advance around a straightforward goal: make enterprise-grade privileged access easier for administrators and users to manage. 

The current One Identity documentation identifies Safeguard for Privileged Passwords 9.0 and Safeguard for Privileged Sessions 9.0 as the latest major releases. The Safeguard 9.0 upgrades include a move to hardware-agnostic deployment, Windows 11 LTSC with embedded licensing for Safeguard for Privileged Passwords, and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS for Safeguard for Privileged Sessions. Software updates are also designed to install faster with less disruption, while session management no longer requires a separate license file simply to continue operating. See the documented Safeguard 9.0 upgrades.

ESXi account discovery reduces manual tracking, while TLS 1.3 and configurable cipher selection make security policies easier to manage and demonstrate during audits. Review the Safeguard 9.0 feature additions. 

This emphasis on reducing operational complexity supports Safeguard’s position among top privileged access management solutions.

item.title: AI-Powered Malware Analysis Uncovers Hidden Phishing Threats and Reduces SOC Workload
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was provided by ANY.RUN. The information and analysis presented are based on their research and findings.

Cybercriminals are using AI to launch more convincing phishing attacks, scale their campaigns, and find new ways to slip past security defenses. For SOC teams, every missed alert or delayed investigation gives attackers more time to steal corporate credentials, access sensitive data, and disrupt business operations.

As investigation queues grow, security leaders face rising operational costs, overloaded analysts, and greater exposure to costly breaches. AI-powered malware analysis is helping organizations uncover hidden threats faster, reduce unnecessary escalations, and handle more incidents without increasing headcount.

Why SOC Teams Are Struggling to Keep Up with Modern Cyberattacks

A single suspicious file or URL can trigger hours of investigation. Analysts must follow redirects, examine suspicious behavior, check related threats, and document their findings before deciding what action to take. As attacks become more complex, these routine tasks take up valuable time that could be spent responding to critical incidents.

These challenges make it harder for SOCs to investigate threats thoroughly without increasing costs or headcount.

How AI Is Changing the Way SOC Teams Investigate Threats

AI-powered malware analysis is taking over some of the most time-consuming parts of security investigations, from following hidden attack chains to connecting related threats and preparing incident reports.

  1. AI-Assisted Automation Exposes Hidden Phishing Attacks

A recent ANY.RUN sandbox investigation shows how AI-assisted automation can uncover hidden attack chains, saving analysts time on repetitive steps while giving them the freedom to take control whenever needed.

The investigation started with a PDF hosted on Adobe’s legitimate platform. Inside, an embedded link led through additional steps, including a CAPTCHA challenge, before revealing a Microsoft OAuth phishing flow targeting corporate accounts.

With Automated Interactivity enabled, the sandbox continued navigating the attack without requiring an analyst to handle every click. The combination of automation and interactivity meant the investigation could continue automatically, while security professionals could step in at any point to inspect suspicious activity or explore other paths.

The SOC Advantage: Less Clicking, More Investigating

Instead of spending time manually reproducing attacks before they can even assess the threat, analysts can focus on suspicious behavior and decisions that require human judgment. This helps security teams investigate more alerts without sacrificing visibility or control.

  1. Related Threat Context Speeds Up Campaign Investigations

Finding one malicious link could be just the beginning. Behind it may be an entire phishing campaign involving dozens of related domains, shared infrastructure, and attacks that have already been investigated elsewhere. Without the right context, security teams risk treating connected threats as isolated incidents.

This is where ANY.RUN’s powerful new Related Threat Context capability changes the investigation. It gives analysts a direct shortcut from a single suspicious indicator to a network of related sandbox analyses, exposing connections across attacks and providing valuable intelligence without starting the investigation from scratch.

In the Adobe PDF investigation, the capability surfaced more than 70 related analyses, helping researchers trace connections to the wider SkyW4lker phishing campaign. Analysts could explore related infrastructure, previous attack activity, and suspicious patterns to better understand the scale of the threat.

The SOC Advantage: Fewer Blind Spots, Faster Response

A single investigation can now provide the context needed to make more informed security decisions. Instead of wasting resources on disconnected alerts, SOC teams can identify which threats are related, prioritize high-risk activity, and focus their response efforts where they matter most. This means fewer missed connections, less repetitive work, and a lower risk of costly incidents.

  1. AI-Generated Reports Turn Complex Findings into Faster SOC Decisions

Uncovering a threat is only half the job. Analysts still need to review the evidence, explain what happened, assess the risks, and document their findings for the next stage of response. Preparing these reports manually can take valuable time, especially when multiple incidents need attention.

AI is now helping reduce this workload. ANY.RUN’s SOC-ready Tier 1 Report automatically brings investigation evidence together and generates an AI Summary explaining the observed malicious behavior, along with AI Recommendations suggesting practical next steps based on the findings.

For example, in the Adobe PDF investigation, the report helps analysts understand the Microsoft OAuth phishing flow, review supporting evidence, and determine what requires further investigation or escalation.

The SOC Advantage: Faster Decisions, Fewer Escalations

With investigation findings and recommended next steps already documented, Tier 1 analysts can make faster decisions without spending hours preparing reports. According to ANY.RUN’s reported customer results, improved investigation workflows can reduce Tier 1 workload by up to 20% and cut Tier 1-to-Tier 2 escalations by 30%, helping security teams respond faster, avoid duplicated work, and reduce the risk of costly incidents.

AI-Powered SOCs: Faster Investigations, Stronger Business Protection

As cybercriminals use AI to make attacks more sophisticated, businesses need to rethink how their security teams work. Detecting a suspicious file or link is only the beginning. What matters is understanding the threat, connecting the evidence, and responding before real damage is done.

AI-powered malware analysis helps security teams do exactly that, taking repetitive work off analysts’ shoulders while keeping them in control of important decisions. This allows organizations to get more out of their existing resources, keep costs under control, and respond to threats with greater confidence.

For security leaders, the goal is simple: give analysts more time to focus on the threats that matter most and prevent small security incidents from turning into costly business problems.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Decade-Old OpenSSH Flaw to Bypass Linux Logins
item.description:
Cybercriminals are exploiting a decade old high-severity vulnerability in OpenSSH that allows them to bypass password authentication on certain Linux systems and install backdoor. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS 8.1) and is nicknamed SSHole. It affects OpenSSH running with the musl C library under specific authentication configurations.

Security researcher Özgün Kültekin discovered  the issue and publicly disclosed it on November 5 when OpenSSH released a fix. The flaw dates back to a 2016 OpenSSH change addressing CVE-2016-6210, a username-enumeration vulnerability that allowed attackers to identify valid accounts by measuring authentication response times.

Understanding the issue

Linux administrators can disable password logins by placing an asterisk (*) in an account’s password field in the /etc/shadow file. However, musl’s crypt() password-hashing function also returns an asterisk when hashing fails, including when someone submits a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

OpenSSH mistakenly treats this error value as a matching password hash and accepts the login. Exploitation requires SSH password authentication to be enabled, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) authentication to be disabled, an account with an asterisk in its password field, and at least one other local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

The flaw affects qualifying musl-based Linux systems, including Alpine Linux and potentially some OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto configurations. Debian and Ubuntu systems using glibc, OpenSSH installations using PAM, and OpenWrt’s default Dropbear SSH server are not affected.

Using Alpine as a container base does not, by itself, expose an application to SSHole. The container must run a reachable, vulnerable SSH server and meet the required authentication conditions.

Some older Alpine Tiny Cloud images for AWS and Azure are particularly exposed because their default alpine account has passwordless doas access, potentially allowing attackers to obtain root access if another account with a valid password hash exists.

Attackers Attempt to Install Python-Based Backdoor

OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, to fix the vulnerability. Public proof-of-concept exploit code appeared roughly four hours later. Security firm watchTowr observed exploitation linked to botnet and cryptocurrency-mining activity on November 6.

GreyNoise detected its first successful SSHole attack on November 7 at 00:46 UTC. The activity involved 18 successful attack chains from six IP addresses targeting GreyNoise’s own vulnerable sensors.

The attackers examined running processes and containers, looked for information exposed through cloud metadata services, and tried to access password hashes and root SSH keys. They also attempted to place their own keys in authorized_keys files to retain access.

After gaining root access in one case, an attacker installed TAC Agent, a Python implant capable of running shell commands, collecting system information and transferring files. GreyNoise says its registration with the command-and-control server failed, and it never received a task. The implant contained Chinese-language comments, logs and error messages, but these do not establish who was behind the attack.

The volume of SSH activity is considerably larger than the confirmed exploitation figures. GreyNoise counted 40.7 million scans of port 22 and 30.1 million attempted SSH sessions, although it could not attribute all this traffic to SSHole.

GreyNoise grouped some of the activity under the name GT10, based on shared infrastructure, tools and actions on compromised systems. The company says other attackers are also exploiting SSHole.

Previdian separately reported 24 exploitation attempts from 15 IP addresses, and also observed activity from 11 countries across four sensors while Finnish security company Defused reported a small number of attackers testing the flaw, although it said the activity was not widespread. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 9.

Update and Patches Details

Though with limited scope, SSHole gives attackers a way to bypass password authentication on vulnerable systems. This makes prompt patching important. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the fix for SSHole.

Administrators should install that version or the patched package supplied by their Linux distribution. Alpine has released fixed packages for versions 3.16 through 3.24, including 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4. After updating, they should restart the SSH service, as installing the package alone does not replace the running daemon.

Administrators who cannot update immediately can disable SSH password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no and restarting the service. They should first verify that SSH key access works.

Security Expert Warns Against Overlooking SSHole Exposure

Ramy Rahman, senior solutions engineer at ArmorCode, shared the following comments with Hackread.com, explaining why the vulnerability could affect more systems than its specific requirements suggest:

“On paper, this is a narrow bug. It only works on a particular kind of lightweight Linux setup, with password logins turned on and a specific account in place. But narrow doesn’t mean small. Alpine is a go-to base image for containers and lightweight infrastructure, so a flaw like this can be baked into hundreds of images that teams may have forgotten they’re running.”

“What makes this one fascinating is that it’s a collision of two perfectly reasonable behaviors. One C library returns an asterisk as an error. Meanwhile, accounts with no password, which is what you want for key-only users, store an asterisk to mean ‘no password.’ The error and the stored value match, and the door opens.”

“Nothing here is a classic memory-safety bug. It’s an assumption mismatch between components, and reportedly it sat there for about a decade, in part because this code is mostly tested on one OS and one C library. It’s a reminder that mainstream software can have blind spots when it runs in less-tested environments.”

“Patch to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s fixed package, and restart sshd, because upgrading the package doesn’t replace the running daemon. That step is easy to miss.”

“But don’t stop at patching. Look back through authentication logs for password logins to accounts that shouldn’t have passwords, and if you can’t rule out a login, treat the host as compromised.”

“Defaults matter. Password authentication is on by default in OpenSSH, so hardening that’s ‘on the list’ is real risk reduction today.”

item.title: TinstaPorn Android Malware Poses as Casino App to Collect User Data
item.description:
A fake Macau casino app uses rigged betting odds to exploit gamblers while collecting phone numbers, location data and device information from Android users.

FortiGuard Labs has analysed a malicious Android application called TinstaPorn, which poses as an online version of a famous casino in Macau. Identified as Android/TinstaPorn.A!tr, the app combines rigged gambling games with the collection of users’ personal information.

In its research shared with Hackread.com, FortiGuard Labs explained that despite its name, TinstaPorn has nothing to do with adult content. It offers casino games such as slots and roulette, but the odds are manipulated in the operators’ favor.

FortiGuard did not explain how the games’ outcomes are manipulated, only noting that the mathematical odds benefit the operators. The platform also encourages users to keep spending through VIP balance top-ups, rebates and referral rewards.

Gambling Comes With a Privacy Risk

The financial losses aren’t the only concern here. FortiGuard found that the application collects phone numbers and precise location information. This includes latitude, longitude, location accuracy and timestamps.

It then sends this information to its game servers through specific communication routes, including /loc/geo-location and /bind_phone. It also sends device identification details and other technical information to a separate logging server. This allows operators to recognize and fingerprint individual devices.

When combined, these details can help operators link a person’s phone number and gambling account to their device and physical location. This creates a privacy risk beyond the money users could lose through the rigged games.

Flutter Makes Malware Analysis Harder

TinstaPorn was developed using Flutter, a Google framework that allows developers to build apps for different platforms (iOS, Android, desktop and web) from the same codebase. FortiGuard noted that the framework also makes malware analysis more difficult because its compiled code does not work like that of typical Android applications.

The challenging aspect is Flutter’s use of a different Application Binary Interface (ABI) as it affects how the app’s code interacts with the underlying system. This can make it harder for analysts to examine the app and understand what it does.

FortiGuard researchers also noted that tools have improved since 2024 with new options available, including r2flutter, Bytecode Studio and AI-assisted analysis through r2ai.

A Multi-Layer Backend Keeps the App Running

Researchers also found a multi-stage server infrastructure supporting the gambling platform. The app first contacts configuration files hosted on GitHub and Gitee. These files provide server addresses rather than executable code.

It then registers the device, contacts line configuration servers to obtain available game server addresses, and stores those details in a local SQLite database. If servers become unavailable, the app has hardcoded alternatives to try. It also tests server response times before selecting a game server.

Communications use AES encryption and HMAC-SHA256 signatures to authenticate requests. However, the AES key is supplied in cleartext by the line configuration server. This means, the encryption mainly obscures traffic rather than protecting it from third-party inspection.

FortiGuard Labs researcher Axelle Apvrille described the operation as more than a basic malware project, concluding that “It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem.”

Deeba Ahmed

item.title: Criminal IP Launches New TI Feed App on Splunkbase for Automated Threat Detection
item.description:
Torrance, USA, November 11th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Criminal IP, the AI-powered threat intelligence and attack surface management platform developed by AI SPERA, has launched the Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk. Available through Splunkbase, the app automatically correlates Criminal IP threat intelligence with firewall traffic logs collected in Splunk.

The integration enables security teams to determine whether organizational assets communicated with malicious IP addresses and whether sessions were successfully established. It also expands Criminal IP’s existing Splunk ecosystem beyond individual IP lookups and fraud detection, helping SOC teams identify high-priority threats within their existing Splunk workflows.

Connecting Threat Intelligence with Network Activity

Security teams often receive large volumes of IP reputation alerts without enough context to determine whether a connection was attempted, blocked, unanswered, or successfully established. This can make it difficult to distinguish routine scanning from communications that require immediate investigation.

The Criminal IP TI Feed app addresses this challenge by correlating inbound and outbound threat intelligence feeds with firewall traffic already indexed in Splunk. Network activity is classified according to observed session outcomes, including completed, unanswered, denied, neutral, and unknown connections.

Severity is also determined using actual firewall activity. Detections without a completed session cannot exceed the watch tier, while critical detections indicate that a session with a malicious IP was successfully established. This helps analysts prioritize incidents with the greatest potential impact.

Automated Correlation and Retrospective Detection

<The Criminal IP TI Feed Overview dashboard in Splunk highlights completed sessions with malicious IP addresses and shows which assets require immediate attention.>

The app downloads Criminal IP TI Feed data every three hours and runs correlation searches against firewall traffic every 10 minutes. Results are written to a dedicated summary index, allowing dashboards and alerts to operate without repeatedly searching large volumes of raw logs.

A daily retrospective search compares the latest Criminal IP threat intelligence against the previous 30 days of firewall traffic. This helps identify historical communications with IP addresses that were not recognized as malicious when the activity originally occurred.

Seven dashboards- Overview, Investigate, All Detections, IP Lookup, Trends, Alerts, and Health- provide visibility into affected assets, malicious IP addresses, traffic direction, session status, severity, detection history, and feed collection health.

The app can also deliver consolidated Slack alerts grouped by malicious IP address and traffic direction. These alerts retain asset-level details, including session counts, timestamps, and transferred data, while throttling repeated notifications to reduce alert fatigue.

Advancing Intelligence-Driven Security Operations

By connecting external threat intelligence with actual network activity, the Criminal IP TI Feed app provides the context analysts need to identify which assets interacted with malicious infrastructure and which detections require immediate attention.

Automating feed collection, log correlation, historical analysis, dashboards, and alerts reduces manual investigation and helps SOC teams respond to meaningful threats more efficiently.

AI SPERA CEO Byungtak Kang stated, “Threat intelligence becomes significantly more actionable when connected to the network activity occurring inside an organization. The Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk helps security teams identify affected assets and prioritize incidents based on observed session behavior.”

About Criminal IP

Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed.

Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake.

Users can learn more and download the app from Splunkbase:

https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/9625
